title: How DNS finds a website
question: How does your browser turn a name like shop.io into an address?

problem.statement: You type shop.io and a page appears. But computers find each other by number (IP addresses), not by name. How does the browser turn a name into an address?
example: Usually answered in a few milliseconds
constraints: Hundreds of millions of names, changing all the time
No single server could hold or answer them all
problem.followUp: Why can a change to a website’s address take hours to reach everyone?

steps.caption: What the interviewer is really asking.

plain.asking: DNS is the internet’s *phone book*: it turns a name like shop.io into the number computers actually use.
points: *You get back:* an IP address, like 203.0.113.7.
*The catch:* no single book holds every name.

steps.caption: Your browser wants shop.io, but the network only delivers to *numbers*. Before anything else, it must find shop.io’s address.
So it asks a *resolver*: a server, run by your internet provider or a public one like 1.1.1.1, that goes and finds the answer for you.

items.label: RESOLVER
items.note: Run by your internet provider, or a public one like 1.1.1.1. It does the asking for you.

steps.caption: The resolver starts at the *root servers*. They don’t know shop.io, but they know who runs every ending, so they reply: “ask the .io servers.”

items.label: RESOLVER
items.note: Run by your internet provider, or a public one like 1.1.1.1. It does the asking for you.

items.label: ROOT SERVERS
items.note: They know who runs every ending: .com, .org, .io and the rest.

items.label: .IO SERVERS
items.note: They know which name server is in charge of each .io name.

items.label: SHOP.IO NAME SERVER
items.note: The authoritative server: it holds the real record for shop.io.

steps.caption: The .io servers don’t know the address either, but they know which *name server* is in charge of shop.io, and point there.

check.question: Which server actually holds the record shop.io → 203.0.113.7?
check.explain: The root and .io servers only *point the way*. The authoritative name server for shop.io is the one that holds the real record.

steps.caption: Billions of lookups a day can’t all walk root → .io → shop.io. The root servers would melt, and every page would wait for three extra round trips.

steps.caption: Every record carries a *TTL*, its time to live, say one hour. A resolver may reuse the answer that long, then must ask again. Browsers and phones cache too.

labels.text: STILL 203.0.113.7 FOR UP TO AN HOUR ✕

steps.caption: Before a move, drop the TTL to, say, 60 seconds and wait for the old hour to pass. Then the switch reaches everyone within a minute.

check.question: You changed shop.io’s address an hour ago, but some users still reach the old server. Why?
options: Their resolvers cached the old answer and its TTL hasn’t run out
DNS changes need a server restart
check.explain: Caches keep an answer until its *TTL* expires. Lower the TTL well before a move so old answers die quickly.

steps.caption: The big idea: DNS is a *chain of referrals* (root → ending → the name’s own server), made fast by caching, and kept fresh by TTLs.
